+status=source_derived_unreviewed; separate FP worker argument and exact rational fixture; frontier capability NOT_ACHIEVED.
+
+Given a complete ideal reversible mass-action reaction list, internal stoichiometric matrix S, positive baseline gates and state relocation factors rho_r(h), define U(S)={gamma : S diag(gamma) K=0} for any basis K of ker S. Every positive gamma in U(S) preserves stationarity of every baseline current in ker S under e'_r=e_r rho_r(h) gamma_r. On edges supporting some kernel current, U(S) consists exactly of scales constant on each column-matroid circuit component. This is conditional on the complete reaction support and the stated mass-action/gate model. It extends N769/N771 common scaling algebra only within that contract; the source producer did not claim this theorem. Historical novelty remains UNKNOWN.
+
+An exact two-pathway Fraction fixture starts with current (1,1,1,1), total gate budget 3 and product ratio 1:1. At target B=3,C=3/2, component scales 30/23 and 10/23 yield gates (30/23,15/23,4/23,20/23), the same total budget and product ratio 3:1. This is a formal steady-state setpoint, not measured selectivity, productivity or process advantage. Direct enzyme allocation/enzyme-cost minimization with the same information is the matched incumbent. A dormant B<->C exchange with gate-rate product 1/100 has zero baseline net current but target residual (-3/200,+3/200), defeating the proposed setpoint and collapsing universal scale freedom from two dimensions to one.
+
+Acquiring a biochemical operation requires complete reaction support including dormant exchange, calibrated reversible laws, state and current measurements, independently actuated gates, reachable and stable target state, reservoir/product control, and a matched costed comparison including sensing, preparation, gate loading, throughput, uncertainty and failures. The optional d=dim ker S current-readout reconstruction pays d independent current observations; it does not provide them for free. N769/N771 original statuses and open physical gates remain.

+status=source_derived_unreviewed; separate FP worker/root sources and same-team review; frontier capability NOT_ACHIEVED.
+
+Classical rare-event gateway: in a stated local-row oracle with N hidden terminal channels, H0 has p0=2^-L/(N+1) and HJ has pJ=2p0. Adaptive random-stopping algorithms giving 1/4 relative error with 2/3 success on every promised instance need at least N/3 expected candidate-terminal queries under H0, or a hard per-run cap of at least N/2. A full N-row scan matches the order. For N=1024,L=8, 288276 iid paths mean about 863702 simulated transitions but about 1125 informative terminal queries; these are different cost units. No atomistic rate or new algorithm is acquired.
+
+Remote response: a local positive frustration-free spin chain with exact product ground has chi_m(e)=(m-1)/m+1/(m^2 e). The e and 2e models have equal first 2m-2 source moments and first differ at moment 2m-1. Unknown-generator evolution-only discrimination costs at least 1/(3e) summed interrogation time under the stated fixed-control model; exact supplied symbolic rows admit an O(m) tridiagonal solve. The worker's mention of N816 is an external, unmerged local lineage at this intake base and is preserved as source wording only. No N816 dependency or canonical status is asserted here.
+
+Routing repair: a proposed DNA frame retains covalent routing junctions and uses reciprocal sacrificial templates to fill eligible gaps. If surviving material admits two different target routings, no repair process seeing only that survivor can infer the lost bit with success above 1/2 on an equal two-world prior. A sufficient abstract restriction is a unique orientation/register-compatible continuation matching with retained, addressable covalent anchors, eligible 3-prime primer and intact template. The all-eligible two-copy patch CTMC has mean loss time (mu+3lambda)/(2lambda^2). If a new lesion is repair-eligible with probability p and ineligible damage remains functional only until the second copy is hit, the exact mean becomes [(3-2p)mu+3lambda]/[2lambda((1-p)mu+lambda)]. At mu/lambda=1000 it falls from 501.5/lambda at p=1 to 46.5/lambda at p=.99. Under independent routing-anchor loss hazard rho, S_frame(T)=exp(-K rho T) S_patch(T)^N; 90% survival with K=100 and lambda T=1 requires rho/lambda<=0.001053605 even before patch failures. These are hypothetical model gates, not measured damage or enzyme rates. Existing matching-staple repair and designed origami gap fill are incumbents. The proposed topology-preserving, no-per-site-staple operation has no physical demonstration or cost advantage.
+
+These are three separate contract-specific results, not a common impossibility theorem. Their executable checks are finite fixtures; correctness, priority and physical transfer remain unreviewed. The decisive tests are (i) acquire hidden reactive-channel information and calibrated entry flux; (ii) pay terminal-coupling precision on an identified sample against same-input solvers; (iii) demonstrate sequence-and-routing restoration in a 2D anchored corridor with anchor-erased controls, chemistry/access checks and a matched full-cost staple-replacement baseline.

+Classical rare-event gateway: in a stated local-row oracle with N hidden terminal channels, H0 has p0=2^-L/(N+1) and HJ has pJ=2p0. Adaptive random-stopping algorithms giving 1/4 relative error with 2/3 success on every promised instance need at least N/3 expected candidate-terminal queries under H0, or a hard per-run cap of at least N/2. A full N-row scan matches the order. For N=1024,L=8, 288276 iid paths mean about 863702 simulated transitions but about 1125 informative terminal queries; these are different cost units. No atomistic rate or new algorithm is acquired.
+
+Remote response: a local positive frustration-free spin chain with exact product ground has chi_m(e)=(m-1)/m+1/(m^2 e). The e and 2e models have equal first 2m-2 source moments and first differ at moment 2m-1. Unknown-generator evolution-only discrimination costs at least 1/(3e) summed interrogation time under the stated fixed-control model; exact supplied symbolic rows admit an O(m) tridiagonal solve. The worker's mention of N816 is an external, unmerged local lineage at this intake base and is preserved as source wording only. No N816 dependency or canonical status is asserted here.
+
+Routing repair: a proposed DNA frame retains covalent routing junctions and uses reciprocal sacrificial templates to fill eligible gaps. If surviving material admits two different target routings, no repair process seeing only that survivor can infer the lost bit with success above 1/2 on an equal two-world prior. A sufficient abstract restriction is a unique orientation/register-compatible continuation matching with retained, addressable covalent anchors, eligible 3-prime primer and intact template. The all-eligible two-copy patch CTMC has mean loss time (mu+3lambda)/(2lambda^2). If a new lesion is repair-eligible with probability p and ineligible damage remains functional only until the second copy is hit, the exact mean becomes [(3-2p)mu+3lambda]/[2lambda((1-p)mu+lambda)]. At mu/lambda=1000 it falls from 501.5/lambda at p=1 to 46.5/lambda at p=.99. Under independent routing-anchor loss hazard rho, S_frame(T)=exp(-K rho T) S_patch(T)^N; 90% survival with K=100 and lambda T=1 requires rho/lambda<=0.001053605 even before patch failures. These are hypothetical model gates, not measured damage or enzyme rates. Existing matching-staple repair and designed origami gap fill are incumbents. The proposed topology-preserving, no-per-site-staple operation has no physical demonstration or cost advantage.
+
+These are three separate contract-specific results, not a common impossibility theorem. Their executable checks are finite fixtures; correctness, priority and physical transfer remain unreviewed. The decisive tests are (i) acquire hidden reactive-channel information and calibrated entry flux; (ii) pay terminal-coupling precision on an identified sample against same-input solvers; (iii) demonstrate sequence-and-routing restoration in a 2D anchored corridor with anchor-erased controls, chemistry/access checks and a matched full-cost staple-replacement baseline.

+## Exact local frustration-free counterfamily
+
+Let `m>=2` qubits form an open chain. Put `n_i=sigma_i^+ sigma_i^-`, and for `1<=i<m` define the **local** annihilation row
+
+```text
+q_i = sigma_i^- - [i/(i+1)] sigma_(i+1)^- .
+H_(m,e) = sum_(i=1)^(m-1) [(i+1)/i] q_i^* q_i + e n_m,
+V = sigma_1^+ + sigma_1^- ,       e>0.
+```
+
+All coefficients are rational when `e` is rational. Every term is positive and has support on at most two adjacent qubits. The vacuum `psi=|0...0>` is annihilated by all rows and is a bond-one MPS. It is the **unique** ground vector: zero energy forces `sigma_m^- phi=0` and every `q_i phi=0`; these linear equations propagate backwards to `sigma_i^- phi=0` for all `i`, whose common kernel is just the vacuum. Neighboring row terms need not commute. The source is exactly `b=|1>` in the one-excitation sector, with `||b||=1` and no ground-space ambiguity.
+
+On basis `|1>,...,|m>`, `H_(m,e)` is the rational tridiagonal `J_(m,e)` with off-diagonal `-1`, diagonals `2` for sites `1,...,m-1`, and terminal diagonal `(m-1)/m+e`. Its first `k<m` leading principal determinants are `k+1`; the full determinant is `m e>0`. Sylvester's criterion gives strict positivity in this source sector. The bottom-right `(m-1)`-square minor has determinant `1/m+(m-1)e`, so Cramer's rule gives the **exact response**
+
+```text
+chi_m(e) = <1|J_(m,e)^(-1)|1> = (m-1)/m + 1/(m^2 e).       (A)
+```
+
+Thus two chains `H_(m,e)` and `H_(m,2e)` have identical product ground states, every row except the terminal `e n_m` term identical, and operator-norm separation `||H_(m,2e)-H_(m,e)||=e`, yet their responses approach a ratio of two as `e -> 0`. More generally `e` versus fixed `c>0` gives an unbounded ratio while retaining identical source-near rows; that comparison has a constant-size remote difference, so it is an information-locality counterexample, not a precision lower bound.
+
+Their source moments `M_k=<b,H^k b>` are **identical for every `0<=k<=2m-2`**. In the walk expansion of `(J^k)_(1,1)`, a term using the changed terminal diagonal must take `m-1` hops to site `m`, use one terminal diagonal step, then take `m-1` hops back. The first possible difference is exactly
+
+```text
+M_(2m-1)(2e) - M_(2m-1)(e) = e.                       (B)
+```
+
+No method whose acquired input consists only of those exact moments, or only rows on sites `1,...,m-1`, can return ±20%-accurate `chi` uniformly for sufficiently small `e`: its inputs are identical while the valid answer intervals are disjoint. This is a **restricted-information impossibility**, not a computational hardness result. Full exact rows expose `e`, and the same-information incumbent computes (A) by a tridiagonal recurrence in `O(m)` rational operations. Supplying that exact row therefore immediately defeats a claimed advantage based on missing gap information.
+
+The conditioning is also exact:
+
+```text
+d chi_m / d t = -1/[m^2 (t-(m-1)/m)^2],  t=(m-1)/m+e.
+```
+
+An absolute uncertainty interval for the terminal coefficient containing both `t_c+e` and `t_c+2e` cannot support a response interval narrower than `[chi_m(2e),chi_m(e)]`. A ground-state MPS witness and exact low-order moments do not repair this coefficient-acquisition requirement.

+In the evolution-only unknown-generator model, the two Hamiltonians differ by `e n_m` of norm `e`. Duhamel's inequality gives `||exp(-it H_1)-exp(-it H_2)||<=e |t|`. Telescoping through arbitrary known controls and adaptive queries (purify measurements) bounds the final trace distance by `e tau`, where `tau` is summed unknown-H evolution time. A protocol returning disjoint ±20% response intervals with success at least `2/3` in each world would distinguish the worlds with success at least `2/3`; Helstrom's bound requires trace distance at least `1/3`. +## 9. A second operation: finite flux-preserving relocation
+
+Independently of the adjoint condition, a mass-action network allows a finite state relocation with no absolute kinetic constants. Keep reservoirs fixed, set c'=c exp(h), and consider a channel with nonzero j_r. Let A_r be its native affinity. Then
+
+\[
+\boxed{\rho_r(h)=\frac{e'_r}{e_r}
+=\frac{1-e^{-A_r}}
+{e^{y_r^Th}-e^{-A_r+y_r'^Th}}.}
+\]
+
+Substitution shows j'_r=j_r. Thus a steady native state gives a steady target state without measuring the individual current magnitudes. Positivity requires that A_r-s_r^Th retain the original sign. A zero-current channel requires s_r^Th=0; its formula is not evaluated as 0/0.
+
+Orient nonzero channels so A_r>0. Then
+
+\[
+\log\rho_r=-y_r^Th+\log(1-e^{-A_r})
+-\log(1-e^{-(A_r-s_r^Th)}).
+\]
+
+This is convex on the thermodynamically feasible halfspace, so the linear enzyme/gate cost sum omega_r e_r rho_r(h) is convex. Scaling every relocated gate by gamma scales all currents by gamma, and under an exactly linear total gate budget the supremal common throughput multiplier is the available budget divided by the infimum relocation cost. It is attained only when an admissible minimiser exists, for example under suitable compact bounds away from forbidden affinity faces. This preserves the entire flux-ratio pattern; it cannot design new flux selectivity.

+
+For any admitted h, write B(h)=sum_r omega_r e_r rho_r(h) and E=sum_r omega_r e_r. The explicit controls
+

+\boxed{e'_r=\frac{E}{B(h)}e_r\rho_r(h)}
+\]
+

At $(i,k)$, $k<L$, move to $(i,k+1)$ with probability $1/2$ and otherwise to absorbing $A$. At $(i,L)$, move deterministically to $B$ if $i$ is reactive and to $A$ otherwise. Conformer 0 is known reactive. The unknown dynamics are either $H_0$, with no additional reactive conformer, or $H_J$, with exactly one additional reactive conformer $J\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$. +## All-adaptive acquisition lower bound
+
+**Proposition, proved for the stated classical local-row oracle.** Any algorithm that meets the $1/4$-relative, $2/3$-success contract on $H_0$ and every $H_J$, including algorithms with adaptive queries and random stopping, makes at least $N/3$ expected candidate-terminal queries on $H_0$. If every execution is capped at $q$ such queries, then $q\geq N/2$. Exact identification in the worst case requires $N$ terminal queries.
+
+**Proof.** Run the algorithm on $H_0$ with all its randomness fixed. Let $S$ be the set of distinct candidate terminal indices queried, and let $E$ be the event that the algorithm outputs a value in the $H_J$ relative-error interval. Correctness on $H_0$ implies $P_0(E)\leq1/3$. Choose $J$ uniformly and couple the run on $H_J$ to the $H_0$ run with identical random bits and oracle replies until terminal state $J$ is queried. Before that query the full transcripts, including all path, splitting, and learning states, are identical. Thus
+
+\[
+P_{J\text{ uniform}}(E)
+\leq P_0(E)+\mathbb E_0\big[|S|\mathbf1_{E^c}\big]/N
+\leq 1/3+\mathbb E_0|S|/N.
+\]
+
+Correctness for every $H_J$ makes the left side at least $2/3$, hence $\mathbb E_0|S|\geq N/3$. If $|S|\leq q$ on every run, retain the $\mathbf1_{E^c}$ factor to get $2/3\leq P_0(E)+(1-P_0(E))q/N\leq1/3+2q/(3N)$, hence $q\geq N/2$. To rule out every possible $J$ with certainty requires all $N$ rows. The expected-cost constant is attainable when $N$ is even: declare $H_J$ without querying on one third of runs; on the other two thirds inspect $N/2$ candidates, declare $H_J$ if found and $H_0$ otherwise. This succeeds with probability $2/3$ in both cases and uses expected $N/3$ terminal calls on $H_0$. The theorem therefore covers arbitrary estimators, not just the attempted tilt. □
+
+The strongest exact classical incumbent for **this** information contract is to evaluate all $N$ unknown terminal rows and compute the rational $p$. It uses $N$ calls, $O(1)$ additional machine words (or $O(n+L)$ bits), and $O(N)$ arithmetic, matching the lower-bound order. FFS, weighted ensembles, adaptive multilevel splitting, learned reaction coordinates, and exact committor linear algebra may eliminate the separate $2^L$ path-barrier factor; the latter still needs the unknown rows. Coherent quantum oracle access changes the interface and admits $O(\sqrt N)$ search via [Grover](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9605043), with an oracle lower bound in [Bennett et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9701001); building that coherent oracle, including state preparation and error control, is not free and was not done here.

+# Follow-up: dual-template DNA-frame repair
+
+## Verdict
+
+A dual-template frame could support *sequence-agnostic, local repair* of a clean single-strand nick or short gap in either strand, provided the opposite strand is continuous across the gap, the damaged strand retains a usable upstream 3′-OH primer and downstream 5′-phosphate, and enzymes can reach the site. Polymerase copies the local sequence already present in the complementary strand; ligase closes the remaining nick. No site-specific repair oligo is needed.
+
+That is a plausible extension of existing DNA repair chemistry, not yet a demonstrated general repair operation for DNA origami. It does not repair an absent whole staple (there is no primer), a double-strand break, a gap in both strands, a damaged/missing template, or all common chemically blocked termini without additional end-processing enzymes. Standard origami also does not provide a continuous complementary strand along every routed segment. The idea becomes experimentally testable if designed as a 2D repair frame with continuous complementary corridors and crossovers kept outside the polymerase path. The largest independent physical gate is enzyme access in folded origami: ligase reaches a practical limit in 3D even for clean, designed nicks.
+
+## What has actually been shown
+

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Exact rational checks for the scoped cycle-scaling construction.
+
+This checks finite examples only. The general statements are proved in REPORT.md.
+"""
+
+from fractions import Fraction as F
+
+
+def rref(matrix):
+    a = [list(map(F, row)) for row in matrix]
+    if not a:
+        return a, []
+    rows, cols = len(a), len(a[0])
+    pivots = []
+    i = 0
+    for j in range(cols):
+        pivot = next((k for k in range(i, rows) if a[k][j]), None)
+        if pivot is None:
+            continue
+        a[i], a[pivot] = a[pivot], a[i]
+        d = a[i][j]
+        a[i] = [x / d for x in a[i]]
+        for k in range(rows):
+            if k != i and a[k][j]:
+                d = a[k][j]
+                a[k] = [x - d * y for x, y in zip(a[k], a[i])]
+        pivots.append(j)
+        i += 1
+        if i == rows:
+            break
+    return a, pivots
+
+
+def kernel(matrix):
+    a, pivots = rref(matrix)
+    if not a:
+        raise ValueError("At least one row is needed")
+    cols = len(a[0])
+    out = []
+    for free in range(cols):
+        if free in pivots:
+            continue
+        v = [F(0) for _ in range(cols)]
+        v[free] = F(1)
+        for row, pivot in enumerate(pivots):
+            v[pivot] = -a[row][free]
+        out.append(v)
+    return out
+
+
+def matvec(matrix, vector):
+    return [sum((F(x) * y for x, y in zip(row, vector)), F(0)) for row in matrix]
+
+
+def universal_scalings(S):
+    k = kernel(S)
+    constraints = []
+    for vector in k:
+        for row in S:
+            constraints.append([F(s) * v for s, v in zip(row, vector)])
+    return kernel(constraints), k
+
+
+def main():
+    independent = [[1, -1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1, -1]]
+    joined = [[1, -1, 0, 0, -1], [0, 0, 1, -1, 1]]
+    independent_scalings, independent_currents = universal_scalings(independent)
+    joined_scalings, joined_currents = universal_scalings(joined)
+    assert len(independent_currents) == 2
+    assert len(independent_scalings) == 2
+    assert len(joined_currents) == 3
+    assert len(joined_scalings) == 1
+
+    # A=4, P=Q=1 are chemostats; B=C=2 at baseline.
+    # Elementary reversible reactions: A<->B, B<->P, A<->C, C<->Q.
+    z0 = [F(2), F(2)]
+    z1 = [F(3), F(3, 2)]
+    gates0 = [F(1, 2), F(1), F(1, 2), F(1)]
+    raw0 = [F(4) - z0[0], z0[0] - F(1), F(4) - z0[1], z0[1] - F(1)]
+    raw1 = [F(4) - z1[0], z1[0] - F(1), F(4) - z1[1], z1[1] - F(1)]
+    j0 = [e * v for e, v in zip(gates0, raw0)]
+    assert j0 == [F(1)] * 4
+    assert matvec(independent, j0) == [F(0), F(0)]
+    rho = [a / b for a, b in zip(raw0, raw1)]
+    assert rho == [F(2), F(1, 2), F(4, 5), F(2)]
+    B1 = sum((gates0[i] * rho[i] for i in (0, 1)), F(0))
+    B2 = sum((gates0[i] * rho[i] for i in (2, 3)), F(0))
+    E = sum(gates0, F(0))
+    target_ratio_multiplier = F(3)
+    gamma2 = E / (target_ratio_multiplier * B1 + B2)
+    gamma1 = target_ratio_multiplier * gamma2
+    assert (B1, B2, E, gamma1, gamma2) == (F(3, 2), F(12, 5), F(3), F(30, 23), F(10, 23))
+    gates1 = [gates0[i] * rho[i] * (gamma1 if i < 2 else gamma2) for i in range(4)]
+    j1 = [e * v for e, v in zip(gates1, raw1)]
+    assert gates1 == [F(30, 23), F(15, 23), F(4, 23), F(20, 23)]
+    assert j1 == [F(30, 23), F(30, 23), F(10, 23), F(10, 23)]
+    assert sum(gates1, F(0)) == E
+    assert matvec(independent, j1) == [F(0), F(0)]
+
+    # An unmodelled B<->C exchange is dormant at baseline and active at the target.
+    eps = F(1, 100)
+    assert eps * (z0[0] - z0[1]) == 0
+    hidden_target_flux = eps * (z1[0] - z1[1])
+    hidden_residual = matvec(joined, j1 + [hidden_target_flux])
+    assert hidden_target_flux == F(3, 200)
+    assert hidden_residual == [F(-3, 200), F(3, 200)]
+
+    print("independent scaling basis:", independent_scalings)
+    print("joined scaling basis:", joined_scalings)
+    print("baseline current:", j0)
+    print("relocation factors:", rho)
+    print("new gates:", gates1)
+    print("new current:", j1)
+    print("total gate budget:", sum(gates1, F(0)))
+    print("hidden reaction target residual:", hidden_residual)
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    main()

Vertices are strand ends or sequence-addressed scaffold intervals; edges record (i) covalent backbone continuation, (ii) crossover routing, and (iii) hybridization of a staple/template interval to its scaffold address. Each edge has strand identity, 5′/3′ orientation, and register. Let (S(G)) be the full scaffold sequence and (K(G)) the surviving covalent routing-junction set after damage (D). The information available to repair is
+
+\[
+O_D(G)=\bigl(S(G),\ \text{surviving strand fragments and their termini},\ \text{template covers},\ K(G)\bigr).
+\]
+
+Two targets are survivor-equivalent when
+
+\[
+G\sim_D G'\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad O_D(G)=O_D(G').
+\]
+
+Exact routing recovery on an allowed target class requires that each survivor-equivalence class contain just one target routing (up to a topology-preserving relabeling that leaves the scientific function unchanged). This condition is necessary: if two different target routings are survivor-equivalent, every repair procedure receives the same input in both cases and cannot return both distinct targets.

+## 3. CTMC formula: correct for its exact assumptions, strongly optimistic as a frame model
+
+Root's states `0 -> 1` at `2 lambda`, `1 -> 0` at `mu`, and `1 -> F` at `lambda` give exactly
+
+```text
+E_0[T_F] = (mu + 3 lambda)/(2 lambda^2).
+```
+
+The generator on transient states is `[[-2lambda,2lambda],[mu,-(mu+lambda)]]`. Its eigenvalues and root's survival formula are correct; `S'(0)=0` and `S(t)|_(mu=0)=2 exp(-lambda t)-exp(-2lambda t)` are independent checks. `S_patch(T)^N` is exact only if patches fail independently with constant rates and each second copy hit at the *same essential locus* ends that patch. Two nonoverlapping strand gaps need not be fatal; a single common-cause lesion or deleted routing junction can be fatal immediately. Neither complication is measured. A shared finite enzyme bath also makes `mu` load-dependent unless throughput and substrate concentration are maintained as the number of patches/devices rises.
+
+Let a new one-copy lesion be eligible for the specified polymerase/ligase path with probability `p`. An ineligible one-copy lesion remains a state `I` that is functional while its other copy persists, but has no repair path: `0 -> R` at `2 lambda p`, `0 -> I` at `2 lambda(1-p)`, `R -> 0` at `mu`, and both `R,I -> F` at `lambda`. This retains the two-copy logic and does **not** call every ineligible hit an immediate failure. First-step equations give the exact extension
+
+```text
+E_0[T_F] = [(3-2p) mu + 3 lambda] /
+           [2 lambda ((1-p) mu + lambda)].                 (1)
+
+lim_(mu->infinity) E_0[T_F]
+  = [1 + 1/(2(1-p))]/lambda,  if p<1.                  (2)
+```
+
+At `mu/lambda=1000`, the all-eligible ideal has mean `501.5/lambda`; with `p=0.99`, (1) gives only `46.5/lambda`, and even infinite repair speed tops out at `51/lambda`. The standard-library exact-rational replay is `repair_review_math.py` with `repair_review_results.json`. This is a **hypothetical countermodel**, not measured lesion chemistry. If a common end-processing bath converts `I` into `R`, that is a genuine route around this bound; its conversion rate, fidelity, side products and resource cost must be acquired. Calling end processing "available if needed" does not supply these values.
+
+Now give each of `K` irreplaceable routing records an independent loss hazard `rho`. In this simple extension,
+
+```text
+S_frame(T) = exp(-K rho T) [S_patch(T)]^N
+             <= exp(-K rho T).                            (3)
+```
+
+For 90% frame survival at horizon `T`, (3) requires `K rho T <= -ln(0.9)=0.1053605...` even with infinitely fast patch repair. If `K=100` and `lambda T=1`, then `rho/lambda <= 0.001053605...`. Root's all-eligible numerical example with `N=100`, `lambda T=1`, `mu/lambda=1000` already gives only `0.81938` patch-frame survival *before* junction loss. With no routing loss, reaching `0.9` in that exact ideal model needs approximately `mu/lambda=1894.245`. These numbers are model thresholds, not rates achieved by an enzyme or frame.
+
+`O(1)` reagent species does not mean `O(1)` material flux. At `N` independent two-copy patches, `2N lambda T` damage events would occur over time `T` while all patches remain fully intact; state occupancy changes the actual count. If a nonvanishing fraction `q` is repaired with mean gap length `ell`, nucleotide demand scales at least as the number of those repaired events times `ell` (approximately `2N lambda T q ell` in the low-occupancy regime), plus enzyme turnover and rejects. For many devices, bath volume/replenishment scales with total attacked material. The fixed per-patch `mu` used in the CTMC silently assumes enough enzyme capacity and dNTP supply to maintain that rate.

+## 4. Strongest incumbents and a decisive paired experiment
+
+The primary [Scheckenbach et al. self-healing study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7986372/) did more than a weak unstabilized control: excess **matching staples** repaired damaged staple features under some conditions, while **nonmatching DNA** provided sacrificial protection; at high 10% FBS stress matching and nonmatching DNA gave comparable stabilization. Its authors explicitly state their exchange mechanism did not repair the long scaffold. Their readouts include AFM and DNA-PAINT geometry, while their strongest molecular inference is still narrower than arbitrary topology restoration. The candidate must beat that same-dose library/protection comparison on *scaffold damage*, its proposed point of difference.
+
+The [designed polymerase gap-filling result](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29451771/) is a direct comparator for prearranged gaps. The use of a small set of common enzymes to process eligible gaps is established biological chemistry: a [purified-protein short-patch repair study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC419455/) reconstituted uracil-lesion repair with glycosylase, APE1, polymerase beta and ligase complex, while a [blocked-end study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3493963/) required PNKP to generate a 3′-OH before gap filling and ligation. These are **duplex DNA substrates, not origami performance demonstrations**. They make a generic common enzyme bath an incumbent chemical mechanism; the candidate's possible advance would be embedding an accessible, route-preserving reciprocal template inside arbitrary frames and sustaining it under unknown damage.
+
+[Keller and colleagues' ligation comparison](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31455950/) reports that ligating accessible staple ends improved origami stability under the tested urea/temperature conditions; it does not establish repair after random damage. [Covalent bonding of designed DNA assemblies](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6097813/) reports greater nuclease resistance with designed crosslinks, while partial terminal/crossover ligation was insufficient for the tested full structure. A more recent [site-specific external crosslinking study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11100008/) shows why function must be matched: external crosslinks can stabilize against some insults yet leave core DNA DNase-accessible. No one of these papers is a complete incumbent for every damage class, but together they prevent comparing only against bare origami.
+
+**Experiment.** Fabricate at least two predeclared frames, one with multiple crossovers, with a fixed target geometry and a function sensitive to route error. Randomize and blind individual, traceable molecules into: (A) reciprocal-template/protected-junction design plus active polymerase, ligase, dNTP and specified end processing; (B) the *same* design and bath composition with the active repair chemistry disabled, to isolate protection; (C) matched conventional origami with optimized excess matching staples plus an equal-mass nonmatching-DNA sacrificial control; (D) the best function-compatible ligated/crosslinked design; and (E) ordinary gap-fill/ligation on a matched design where it can act. Match exposure, temperature, total DNA mass, handling and cost. Predeclare a mixed lesion challenge including eligible scaffold and staple gaps, blocked ends, overlapping opposite-strand lesions, junction hits and a realistic random-damage regime. Do not select only successful/eligible molecules after the challenge. Measure eligibility `p`, junction survival `rho`, repair kinetics `mu`, and lesion rates from sacrificial characterization cohorts, with confidence intervals and end chemistry, rather than assuming them from the ideal CTMC.
+
+For the **same tracked molecules**, require evidence of newly synthesized sequence spanning a known scaffold gap and a restored covalent join, a correct junction/strand-continuity map, restored 3D geometry, and recovered function over repeated blinded damage/repair cycles. Pulse-labeled nucleotide incorporation alone can mark free or irrelevant DNA; fluorescence alone can persist on a misrouted frame. Use appropriate sequence/ligation assays and single-particle imaging or equivalent complementary readouts, with before/after lineage so survival of undamaged molecules or reassembly cannot masquerade as repair. Record denominator and uncertainty for each lesion class and for the full mixed challenge.
+
+**Kill criteria.** The proposed capability fails its stated unknown-damage scope if scaffold lesions are not covalently repaired in the same tracked frame, if route/geometry/function recovery is not established, or if success is confined to preselected eligible gaps and does not survive the full challenge denominator. It fails a new-operation advantage claim if active chemistry adds no verified recovery above (B), if the gain is matched by same-dose excess staples/sacrificial DNA or function-compatible ligation/crosslinking after full costs, or if per-defect primers/route-specific replacement species are needed in the bath. A protected route with measured `K rho T` already exceeding the target survival budget in (3) kills the claimed frame-lifetime target regardless of `mu`. These conditions do not erase a narrower proof-of-principle for designed gaps; they prevent promoting it as arbitrary, repeated, common-bath repair.

+## New conditional operation and maximal boundary
+
+Define the *rate-free scaling space*
+
+`U(S)={gamma in R^m : S diag(gamma) K=0}`, where the columns of `K` form any basis of `ker S`.
+
+This is a computable linear space independent of the unknown current. Every positive `gamma in U(S)` preserves stationarity for **every** current in `ker S`, hence for every baseline compatible with the complete model. Scalar multiples of `1` are always present; N771 uses only these. My extension allows distinct positive scales on separate support components. For fixed `h`, the total gate cost `sum_r w_r e_r rho_r(h) gamma_r` and each cap are linear in `gamma`. If `gamma` is parameterized by one positive scalar per circuit component, then `t_a=log gamma_a` gives the same convex upper-budget structure as N771 because each `log rho_r(h)` is convex in `h`. The resulting selected product ratio between two components is multiplied by `gamma_a/gamma_b`. Absolute productivity still requires a measured baseline flux.
+
+**Maximality theorem, within this information contract.** Let a circuit of `S` mean a support-minimal nonzero vector in `ker S`, and join reaction indices when they lie in one circuit; take transitive closure. On all reaction indices that can carry a nonzero stationary current, `gamma in U(S)` iff `gamma` is constant on each such circuit component. A reaction outside every circuit carries zero in every vector of `ker S`, so its scale is irrelevant to the steady current. Proof: for a circuit vector `v`, both `v` and `diag(gamma)v` lie in `ker S`; the kernel supported on that minimal support is one-dimensional, forcing equal `gamma` on every nonzero coordinate. Transitive closure gives necessity. Conversely, every kernel vector is a linear combination of circuit vectors (remove a support-minimal dependence iteratively), and a componentwise-constant diagonal map sends each circuit vector to a scalar multiple of itself. Thus it preserves all of `ker S`. If physically possible currents occupy only a smaller subspace, this theorem is conservative; with a strictly positive point in the oriented flux cone, that cone spans `ker S`, so the boundary is exact for all such currents.
+
+This theorem is a narrow algebraic observation, and the connection to known flux modes and network localization makes historical novelty **UNKNOWN**. It is not a universal biological controllability result. A coupled network whose column-dependence matroid is connected admits only N771's common scale when no current magnitudes are known. Thus topology itself says when the hoped-for rate-free change in selectivity is impossible under the universal guarantee.
+
+There is a second, paid escape hatch. If `d=dim ker S`, choose `d` individual current measurements whose coordinate projection `P K` is nonsingular; such a choice exists because `K` has rank `d`. Then `j=K(PK)^{-1}Pj`, and any desired positive, same-orientation `j* in ker S` can be compiled at the target state by `e'_r=e_r rho_r(h) j*_r/j_r`. With fewer than `d` independent linear current readings, generic full-current reconstruction is impossible: two nearby currents in the positive relative interior of the flux cone can share those readings but require different gate ratios for a fixed `j*`. This is a lower bound for **full-current, fixed-target compilation** under that measurement interface; it is not a lower bound for a chosen ratio, for which far fewer measurements may suffice. Near-zero currents and a poorly conditioned `PK` can make the nominally low-dimensional readout very expensive. If `hat j=j+delta`, the actual stationarity residual under the compiled gates is `-S diag(j*/hat j) delta`, so a valid error bound requires acquired `|j_r|` margins and readout errors.

Those systems are **not** instances established to meet the ideal model below. +
+Define the *rate-free scaling space*

+`U(S)={gamma in R^m : S diag(gamma) K=0}`, where the columns of `K` form any basis of `ker S`.

+This is a computable linear space independent of the unknown current. Every positive `gamma in U(S)` preserves stationarity for **every** current in `ker S`, hence for every baseline compatible with the complete model. Scalar multiples of `1` are always present; N771 uses only these. My extension allows distinct positive scales on separate support components. For fixed `h`, the total gate cost `sum_r w_r e_r rho_r(h) gamma_r` and each cap are linear in `gamma`. If `gamma` is parameterized by one positive scalar per circuit component, then `t_a=log gamma_a` gives the same convex upper-budget structure as N771 because each `log rho_r(h)` is convex in `h`. +**Maximality theorem, within this information contract.** Let a circuit of `S` mean a support-minimal nonzero vector in `ker S`, and join reaction indices when they lie in one circuit; take transitive closure. A reaction outside every circuit carries zero in every vector of `ker S`, so its scale is irrelevant to the steady current. Proof: for a circuit vector `v`, both `v` and `diag(gamma)v` lie in `ker S`; the kernel supported on that minimal support is one-dimensional, forcing equal `gamma` on every nonzero coordinate. Transitive closure gives necessity. Conversely, every kernel vector is a linear combination of circuit vectors (remove a support-minimal dependence iteratively), and a componentwise-constant diagonal map sends each circuit vector to a scalar multiple of itself. Thus it preserves all of `ker S`. +#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Exact rational checks for the scoped cycle-scaling construction.
+
+This checks finite examples only. The general statements are proved in REPORT.md.
+"""
+
+from fractions import Fraction as F
+
+
+def rref(matrix):
+    a = [list(map(F, row)) for row in matrix]
+    if not a:
+        return a, []
+    rows, cols = len(a), len(a[0])
+    pivots = []
+    i = 0
+    for j in range(cols):
+        pivot = next((k for k in range(i, rows) if a[k][j]), None)
+        if pivot is None:
+            continue
+        a[i], a[pivot] = a[pivot], a[i]
+        d = a[i][j]
+        a[i] = [x / d for x in a[i]]
+        for k in range(rows):
+            if k != i and a[k][j]:
+                d = a[k][j]
+                a[k] = [x - d * y for x, y in zip(a[k], a[i])]
+        pivots.append(j)
+        i += 1
+        if i == rows:
+            break
+    return a, pivots
+
+
+def kernel(matrix):
+    a, pivots = rref(matrix)
+    if not a:
+        raise ValueError("At least one row is needed")
+    cols = len(a[0])
+    out = []
+    for free in range(cols):
+        if free in pivots:
+            continue
+        v = [F(0) for _ in range(cols)]
+        v[free] = F(1)
+        for row, pivot in enumerate(pivots):
+            v[pivot] = -a[row][free]
+        out.append(v)
+    return out
+
+
+def matvec(matrix, vector):
+    return [sum((F(x) * y for x, y in zip(row, vector)), F(0)) for row in matrix]
+
+
+def universal_scalings(S):
+    k = kernel(S)
+    constraints = []
+    for vector in k:
+        for row in S:
+            constraints.append([F(s) * v for s, v in zip(row, vector)])
+    return kernel(constraints), k
+
+
+def main():
+    independent = [[1, -1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1, -1]]
+    joined = [[1, -1, 0, 0, -1], [0, 0, 1, -1, 1]]
+    independent_scalings, independent_currents = universal_scalings(independent)
+    joined_scalings, joined_currents = universal_scalings(joined)
+    assert len(independent_currents) == 2
+    assert len(independent_scalings) == 2
+    assert len(joined_currents) == 3
+    assert len(joined_scalings) == 1
+
+    # A=4, P=Q=1 are chemostats; B=C=2 at baseline.
+    # Elementary reversible reactions: A<->B, B<->P, A<->C, C<->Q.
+    z0 = [F(2), F(2)]
+    z1 = [F(3), F(3, 2)]
+    gates0 = [F(1, 2), F(1), F(1, 2), F(1)]
+    raw0 = [F(4) - z0[0], z0[0] - F(1), F(4) - z0[1], z0[1] - F(1)]
+    raw1 = [F(4) - z1[0], z1[0] - F(1), F(4) - z1[1], z1[1] - F(1)]
+    j0 = [e * v for e, v in zip(gates0, raw0)]
+    assert j0 == [F(1)] * 4
+    assert matvec(independent, j0) == [F(0), F(0)]
+    rho = [a / b for a, b in zip(raw0, raw1)]
+    assert rho == [F(2), F(1, 2), F(4, 5), F(2)]
+    B1 = sum((gates0[i] * rho[i] for i in (0, 1)), F(0))
+    B2 = sum((gates0[i] * rho[i] for i in (2, 3)), F(0))
+    E = sum(gates0, F(0))
+    target_ratio_multiplier = F(3)
+    gamma2 = E / (target_ratio_multiplier * B1 + B2)
+    gamma1 = target_ratio_multiplier * gamma2
+    assert (B1, B2, E, gamma1, gamma2) == (F(3, 2), F(12, 5), F(3), F(30, 23), F(10, 23))
+    gates1 = [gates0[i] * rho[i] * (gamma1 if i < 2 else gamma2) for i in range(4)]
+    j1 = [e * v for e, v in zip(gates1, raw1)]
+    assert gates1 == [F(30, 23), F(15, 23), F(4, 23), F(20, 23)]
+    assert j1 == [F(30, 23), F(30, 23), F(10, 23), F(10, 23)]
+    assert sum(gates1, F(0)) == E
+    assert matvec(independent, j1) == [F(0), F(0)]
+
+    # An unmodelled B<->C exchange is dormant at baseline and active at the target.
+    eps = F(1, 100)
+    assert eps * (z0[0] - z0[1]) == 0
+    hidden_target_flux = eps * (z1[0] - z1[1])
+    hidden_residual = matvec(joined, j1 + [hidden_target_flux])
+    assert hidden_target_flux == F(3, 200)
+    assert hidden_residual == [F(-3, 200), F(3, 200)]
+
+    print("independent scaling basis:", independent_scalings)
+    print("joined scaling basis:", joined_scalings)
+    print("baseline current:", j0)
+    print("relocation factors:", rho)

+# Computation lane: a hidden-channel gate for certified rare-event rates
+
+**Status: no new frontier operation established.** I pursued a certificate-carrying committor/Doob-tilt operation for a scientifically important output: a rare transition probability, the ingredient needed with an independently measured entry flux to obtain a nucleation or reaction rate. A small exact model shows why its apparent gain fails after charging acquisition of unseen reactive channels. The result is an oracle obstruction, not a claim about a real material or a novelty claim.
+
+This was an instructed independent initial investigation. Isolation from other workers was a workflow instruction, not an enforced technical boundary. I read the campaign brief and capital entry instructions, but did not read another current worker's report or use a historical capital claim as a premise.
+
+## Output, information, and resources
+
+The desired output is $p=P_s(\tau_B<\tau_A)$ to relative error at most $1/4$, with success probability at least $2/3$ for every admissible dynamics. A physical rate would be $\lambda p$, where the entry flux $\lambda$ must be acquired and calibrated separately; no value of $\lambda$, force field, experimental rate, or atomistic result is claimed here. Actual crystal nucleation rates are computed using forward flux sampling in [Jiang et al.'s NaCl study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.07804); its force-field rates did not agree with the cited experiments, underscoring the need to separate a model rate from physical validation.
+
+For the exact comparison, let $N=2^n$ candidate conformers and $L\geq0$ barrier stages. From $s$, choose $i\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$ uniformly. At $(i,k)$, $k<L$, move to $(i,k+1)$ with probability $1/2$ and otherwise to absorbing $A$. At $(i,L)$, move deterministically to $B$ if $i$ is reactive and to $A$ otherwise. Conformer 0 is known reactive. The unknown dynamics are either $H_0$, with no additional reactive conformer, or $H_J$, with exactly one additional reactive conformer $J\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$. All labels, graph structure, stage probabilities, and the transition rule for 0 are supplied. The only unknown is the $N$-bit terminal reaction rule, promised to contain zero or one additional 1.
+
+The acquisition interface is deliberately generous: an algorithm may choose **any** state and obtain its exact local transition row at unit cost. It can also generate paths, clone them, choose levels, query adaptively, randomize, and stop at a random time. State preparation, simulation of the known stages, and arithmetic are free in the lower bound. This is stronger than a forward-only molecular simulator. A full transition table or a source program exposing $J$ is *not* supplied. Total transition-row calls are the work measure; parallel calls reduce wall time only with proportional hardware. Query labels require $O(n+\log L)$ bits and exact output fractions require $O(n+L)$ bits. Charging force-field construction, experimental calibration, memory/communication, finite precision, and energy would increase costs, not remove the lower bound.
+
+The exact answers are
+
+\[
+p_0=\frac{2^{-L}}{N+1},\qquad p_J=\frac{2^{1-L}}{N+1}=2p_0.
+\]
+
+The two allowed relative-error intervals, $[3p_0/4,5p_0/4]$ and $[3p_0/2,5p_0/2]$, are disjoint.
+
+## Attempted operation and the actual gate
+
+The attempted operation learns a trial committor $v$ from short paths, tilts trajectories toward $B$, and corrects the rate using a stopped residual. For an absorbing Markov chain and $v(A)=0,v(B)=1$, the exact identity is
+
+\[
+q(s)=v(s)+\mathbb E_s\!\left[\sum_{t<\tau_A\wedge\tau_B}(Pv-v)(X_t)\right]. \tag{1}
+\]
+
+For each stopped path, telescope $v(X_\tau)-v(s)$, condition each increment on its current state, and use $v(X_\tau)=\mathbf1_{\{X_\tau=B\}}$. This proves (1) without a model approximation.
+
+If $v=q$, the Doob transition $P^q(x,y)=P(x,y)q(y)/q(x)$ on positive-$q$ states samples conditioned reactive paths with constant likelihood weight. That is the strongest conceptual comparator, not an invention here. Existing work already develops forward-flux efficiency calculations, statistically exact weighted ensembles, lag-corrected variational committors, and committor-based optimal control: [Allen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0602269), [Zhang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.1963), [Lorpaiboon et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03539), and [Du et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13213). These are primary sources; I inspected accessible abstracts and the 2025 committor paper's methods, not every implementation or dataset.
+
+On $H_0$, a learned baseline can be exact: $v=q_0$. On $H_J$, the *same* $v$ has residual zero at every transient state except $(J,L)$, where $(Pv-v)(J,L)=1$. Thus every path or validation query that misses $J$ reports a perfectly harmonic candidate, while (1) still has an omitted correction $p_0$: the claimed rate is wrong by a factor of two. Ordinary forward paths see that residual with probability $p_0$. An exact empirical zero-residual finding on visited states is therefore not a global certificate.
+
+Even granting **perfect, free conditioning through all $L$ barrier stages**, the unseen-channel cost remains. Let an importance proposal assign branch probabilities proportional to $1,\epsilon,\ldots,\epsilon$, with the known branch weighted 1 and every unknown branch weighted $\epsilon>0$. Under $H_J$, the unbiased estimator is $Y=2^{-L}\mathbf1_{\{I\in\{0,J\}\}}/((N+1)r_I)$ when branch $I$ is sampled from proposal $r$. Its relative variance is exactly
+
+\[
+\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}{p_J^2}
+=\frac{(1+N\epsilon)(1+\epsilon^{-1})}{4}-1.
+\]
+
+Only the base and hidden branches contribute to $\mathbb E Y^2$, giving $\mathbb E Y^2=2^{-2L}(r_0^{-1}+r_J^{-1})/(N+1)^2$; divide by $p_J^2=4\cdot2^{-2L}/(N+1)^2$.
+
+Its best symmetric choice is $\epsilon=N^{-1/2}$, giving $(N+2\sqrt N-3)/4=\Theta(N)$. The uniform choice gives $(N-1)/2$. Setting $\epsilon=0$ omits the hidden path and makes the estimate biased rather than zero variance. Learning a good tilt on observed paths does not pay for finding an unobserved channel.
+
+## All-adaptive acquisition lower bound
+
+**Proposition, proved for the stated classical local-row oracle.** Any algorithm that meets the $1/4$-relative, $2/3$-success contract on $H_0$ and every $H_J$, including algorithms with adaptive queries and random stopping, makes at least $N/3$ expected candidate-terminal queries on $H_0$. If every execution is capped at $q$ such queries, then $q\geq N/2$. Exact identification in the worst case requires $N$ terminal queries.
+
+**Proof.** Run the algorithm on $H_0$ with all its randomness fixed. Let $S$ be the set of distinct candidate terminal indices queried, and let $E$ be the event that the algorithm outputs a value in the $H_J$ relative-error interval. Correctness on $H_0$ implies $P_0(E)\leq1/3$. Choose $J$ uniformly and couple the run on $H_J$ to the $H_0$ run with identical random bits and oracle replies until terminal state $J$ is queried. Before that query the full transcripts, including all path, splitting, and learning states, are identical. Thus
+
+\[
+P_{J\text{ uniform}}(E)
+\leq P_0(E)+\mathbb E_0\big[|S|\mathbf1_{E^c}\big]/N
+\leq 1/3+\mathbb E_0|S|/N.
+\]
+
+Correctness for every $H_J$ makes the left side at least $2/3$, hence $\mathbb E_0|S|\geq N/3$. If $|S|\leq q$ on every run, retain the $\mathbf1_{E^c}$ factor to get $2/3\leq P_0(E)+(1-P_0(E))q/N\leq1/3+2q/(3N)$, hence $q\geq N/2$. To rule out every possible $J$ with certainty requires all $N$ rows. The expected-cost constant is attainable when $N$ is even: declare $H_J$ without querying on one third of runs; on the other two thirds inspect $N/2$ candidates, declare $H_J$ if found and $H_0$ otherwise. This succeeds with probability $2/3$ in both cases and uses expected $N/3$ terminal calls on $H_0$. The theorem therefore covers arbitrary estimators, not just the attempted tilt. □
+
+The strongest exact classical incumbent for **this** information contract is to evaluate all $N$ unknown terminal rows and compute the rational $p$. It uses $N$ calls, $O(1)$ additional machine words (or $O(n+L)$ bits), and $O(N)$ arithmetic, matching the lower-bound order. FFS, weighted ensembles, adaptive multilevel splitting, learned reaction coordinates, and exact committor linear algebra may eliminate the separate $2^L$ path-barrier factor; the latter still needs the unknown rows. Coherent quantum oracle access changes the interface and admits $O(\sqrt N)$ search via [Grover](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9605043), with an oracle lower bound in [Bennett et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9701001); building that coherent oracle, including state preparation and error control, is not free and was not done here.

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Exact finite audit of a hidden-channel rare-event computation contract.
+
+This is an arithmetic check and transparent comparator, not molecular data.
+All counts charge calls to the classical local transition oracle.
+"""
+
+from fractions import Fraction
+from itertools import combinations
+import json
+import math
+
+
+def rate(candidate_count: int, barrier_levels: int, gateway_count: int) -> Fraction:
+    return Fraction(gateway_count, (candidate_count + 1) * (1 << barrier_levels))
+
+
+def relative_importance_variance(candidate_count: int, epsilon: Fraction) -> Fraction:
+    """Variance/mean^2 with a known gateway plus one hidden gateway.
+
+    Proposal branch probabilities are proportional to (1, epsilon, ..., epsilon).
+    The barrier factor is assumed removed perfectly, favouring the proposal.
+    """
+    n = candidate_count
+    assert epsilon > 0
+    proposal_base = Fraction(1, 1) / (1 + n * epsilon)
+    proposal_other = epsilon / (1 + n * epsilon)
+    probability = Fraction(2, n + 1)
+    second_moment = (
+        Fraction(1, proposal_base) + Fraction(1, proposal_other)
+    ) / (n + 1) ** 2
+    closed_form = (1 + n * epsilon) * (1 + 1 / epsilon) / 4 - 1
+    answer = second_moment / probability**2 - 1
+    assert answer == closed_form
+    return answer
+
+
+def exhaustive_coverage_audit() -> int:
+    cases = 0
+    for n in range(2, 9):
+        for q in range(n + 1):
+            for selected in combinations(range(1, n + 1), q):
+                discoveries = sum(j in selected for j in range(1, n + 1))
+                assert Fraction(discoveries, n) == Fraction(q, n)
+                cases += 1
+    return cases
+
+
+def direct_draws_for_two_thirds(delta: Fraction) -> int:
+    """Minimum iid forward trajectories to hit the extra channel with probability 2/3."""
+    target = math.log(1 / 3) / math.log1p(-float(delta))
+    count = math.ceil(target)
+    # Float logarithms choose a nearby integer; verify the threshold exactly.
+    while (1 - delta) ** count > Fraction(1, 3):
+        count += 1
+    while count > 0 and (1 - delta) ** (count - 1) <= Fraction(1, 3):
+        count -= 1
+    return count
+
+
+def main() -> None:
+    levels = 8
+    rows = []
+    for n in (64, 256, 1024):
+        root = math.isqrt(n)
+        assert root * root == n
+        p0 = rate(n, levels, 1)
+        p1 = rate(n, levels, 2)
+        delta = p1 - p0
+        epsilon_opt = Fraction(1, root)
+        direct_draws = direct_draws_for_two_thirds(delta)
+        # One start transition, a truncated geometric number of barrier moves,
+        # and a terminal move only when every barrier stage is crossed.
+        expected_steps_per_forward_path = Fraction(3) - Fraction(1, 1 << levels)
+        expected_unknown_terminal_calls_per_forward_path = Fraction(
+            n, (n + 1) * (1 << levels)
+        )
+        rows.append(
+            {
+                "candidate_count": n,
+                "barrier_levels": levels,
+                "p0_exact": str(p0),
+                "p1_exact": str(p1),
+                "p0_decimal": float(p0),
+                "p1_decimal": float(p1),
+                "all_terminal_queries_for_exact_answer": n,
+                "random_stopping_min_expected_terminal_queries_under_H0": f"{n}/3",
+                "fixed_query_min_terminal_queries_for_two_thirds": n // 2,
+                "direct_forward_trajectories_for_two_thirds_extra_channel_detection": direct_draws,
+                "direct_expected_all_transition_evaluations_at_fixed_trial_count": float(
+                    direct_draws * expected_steps_per_forward_path
+                ),
+                "direct_expected_unknown_terminal_queries_at_fixed_trial_count": float(
+                    direct_draws * expected_unknown_terminal_calls_per_forward_path
+                ),
+                "relative_variance_uniform_branch_proposal": str(relative_importance_variance(n, Fraction(1))),
+                "relative_variance_best_symmetric_branch_proposal": str(relative_importance_variance(n, epsilon_opt)),
+                "best_symmetric_epsilon": str(epsilon_opt),
+            }
+        )
+    print(json.dumps({"exhaustive_coverage_cases": exhaustive_coverage_audit(), "rows": rows}, indent=2))
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    main()

+# Adversarial boundary: local response needs remote precision
+
+15 October 2026, Brisbane. Independent adversarial investigation as instructed in `BRIEF.txt`; isolation from other workers was instructed, not technically enforced. No other current worker report was consulted. **Capability status: NOT ACHIEVED.** The new result here is a self-contained counterfamily and an access-model lower bound, not a winning physical or computational operation. Originality of the counterfamily is **UNKNOWN** pending a dedicated literature review.
+
+## Scientific output and exact interface
+
+The consequential target is a *certified, material-specific zero-temperature local static response* near a small excitation scale, enough to distinguish a factor-two difference (say a ±20% response interval). Such a response is the curvature of ground energy under a local field and can inform field-tuned quantum critical physics. This relevance is supported by the primary quantum-critical susceptibility analysis of [Fischer and Rosch, Phys. Rev. B 71, 184429 (2005)](https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.71.184429). Our exact models below are engineered spin chains, **not** acquired materials or evidence of a new quantum-critical experiment. We do not assert that current methods cannot measure susceptibility in actual materials: [experimental susceptibility at a field-tuned transition](https://journals.aps.org/prmaterials/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.6.094413) already exists. The missing output is a *rigorous local zero-temperature interval from an uncertain microscopic input* at an independently demonstrated useful cost.
+
+For a positive local Hamiltonian `H` with unique normalized ground vector `psi`, and local Hermitian `V` with zero ground expectation, the convention is `b=V psi`, `chi=<b,H^+ b>`, and ground-energy second derivative `E''(0)=-2 chi` for `H+lambda V`. Two input models matter:
+
+1. **Exact symbolic rows supplied:** coefficients of all local terms and the ground state are exact. A conventional solver may inspect every row and use any exact algebra.
+2. **Unknown physical generator acquired only through controlled evolution:** all known controls, preparation, measurements and ancillas are allowed, but dependence on the unknown `H` enters through evolutions of total interrogation time `tau` (summed over parallel copies). Additional direct coefficient metrology is a different acquisition channel whose precision, preparation, calibration and cost must be charged. The lower bound below applies only to this stated model.
+
+Existing response competitors include correction-vector DMRG, MPS linear response, Lanczos/Gauss quadrature, exact low-dimensional inversion and gap/SDP certificates. [Nakatani et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.1646) give established DMRG linear-response algorithms; [Golub and Strakoš](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02142693) treat inverse quadratic forms using Gauss-type quadrature. A new finite-moment or local-row method cannot claim priority for response or inverse-form bounds by rephrasing these operations.
+
+## Exact local frustration-free counterfamily
+
+Let `m>=2` qubits form an open chain. Put `n_i=sigma_i^+ sigma_i^-`, and for `1<=i<m` define the **local** annihilation row
+
+```text
+q_i = sigma_i^- - [i/(i+1)] sigma_(i+1)^- .
+H_(m,e) = sum_(i=1)^(m-1) [(i+1)/i] q_i^* q_i + e n_m,
+V = sigma_1^+ + sigma_1^- ,       e>0.
+```
+
+All coefficients are rational when `e` is rational. Every term is positive and has support on at most two adjacent qubits. The vacuum `psi=|0...0>` is annihilated by all rows and is a bond-one MPS. It is the **unique** ground vector: zero energy forces `sigma_m^- phi=0` and every `q_i phi=0`; these linear equations propagate backwards to `sigma_i^- phi=0` for all `i`, whose common kernel is just the vacuum. Neighboring row terms need not commute. The source is exactly `b=|1>` in the one-excitation sector, with `||b||=1` and no ground-space ambiguity.
+
+On basis `|1>,...,|m>`, `H_(m,e)` is the rational tridiagonal `J_(m,e)` with off-diagonal `-1`, diagonals `2` for sites `1,...,m-1`, and terminal diagonal `(m-1)/m+e`. Its first `k<m` leading principal determinants are `k+1`; the full determinant is `m e>0`. Sylvester's criterion gives strict positivity in this source sector. The bottom-right `(m-1)`-square minor has determinant `1/m+(m-1)e`, so Cramer's rule gives the **exact response**
+
+```text
+chi_m(e) = <1|J_(m,e)^(-1)|1> = (m-1)/m + 1/(m^2 e).       (A)
+```
+
+Thus two chains `H_(m,e)` and `H_(m,2e)` have identical product ground states, every row except the terminal `e n_m` term identical, and operator-norm separation `||H_(m,2e)-H_(m,e)||=e`, yet their responses approach a ratio of two as `e -> 0`. More generally `e` versus fixed `c>0` gives an unbounded ratio while retaining identical source-near rows; that comparison has a constant-size remote difference, so it is an information-locality counterexample, not a precision lower bound.
+
+Their source moments `M_k=<b,H^k b>` are **identical for every `0<=k<=2m-2`**. In the walk expansion of `(J^k)_(1,1)`, a term using the changed terminal diagonal must take `m-1` hops to site `m`, use one terminal diagonal step, then take `m-1` hops back. The first possible difference is exactly
+
+```text
+M_(2m-1)(2e) - M_(2m-1)(e) = e.                       (B)
+```
+
+No method whose acquired input consists only of those exact moments, or only rows on sites `1,...,m-1`, can return ±20%-accurate `chi` uniformly for sufficiently small `e`: its inputs are identical while the valid answer intervals are disjoint. This is a **restricted-information impossibility**, not a computational hardness result. Full exact rows expose `e`, and the same-information incumbent computes (A) by a tridiagonal recurrence in `O(m)` rational operations. Supplying that exact row therefore immediately defeats a claimed advantage based on missing gap information.
+
+The conditioning is also exact:
+
+```text
+d chi_m / d t = -1/[m^2 (t-(m-1)/m)^2],  t=(m-1)/m+e.
+```
+
+An absolute uncertainty interval for the terminal coefficient containing both `t_c+e` and `t_c+2e` cannot support a response interval narrower than `[chi_m(2e),chi_m(e)]`. A ground-state MPS witness and exact low-order moments do not repair this coefficient-acquisition requirement.
+
+## Physical acquisition lower bound
+
+In the evolution-only unknown-generator model, the two Hamiltonians differ by `e n_m` of norm `e`. Duhamel's inequality gives `||exp(-it H_1)-exp(-it H_2)||<=e |t|`. Telescoping through arbitrary known controls and adaptive queries (purify measurements) bounds the final trace distance by `e tau`, where `tau` is summed unknown-H evolution time. A protocol returning disjoint ±20% response intervals with success at least `2/3` in each world would distinguish the worlds with success at least `2/3`; Helstrom's bound requires trace distance at least `1/3`. Hence
+
+```text
+tau >= 1/(3e).                                        (C)
+```
+
+With physical units this is `hbar/(3e)`. Parallel copies can lower wall-clock duration but not summed interrogation time; preparation, controls, readout and calibration only add cost. The bound has the expected Heisenberg precision dependence. [Huang, Tong, Fang and Su](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03030) already give Hamiltonian learning at total evolution time `O(1/e)` together with a matching lower-bound scope. This source supports treating the order `1/e` benchmark as incumbent performance, not our novelty. The elementary proof above is a specific two-world derivation.
+

+"""Exact rational replay of the remote-row susceptibility boundary.
+
+No external dependencies. Run: python3 verify_boundary.py
+"""
+
+from fractions import Fraction as F
+import json
+
+
+def matrix(m, gap):
+    """One-excitation matrix of the local frustration-free chain."""
+    assert m >= 2 and gap > 0
+    terminal = F(m - 1, m) + gap
+    j = [[F(0) for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
+    for i in range(m):
+        j[i][i] = F(2) if i < m - 1 else terminal
+        if i + 1 < m:
+            j[i][i + 1] = j[i + 1][i] = F(-1)
+    return j
+
+
+def multiply(a, b):
+    n = len(a)
+    return [[sum(a[i][k] * b[k][j] for k in range(n))
+             for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
+
+
+def moments(j, end):
+    n = len(j)
+    power = [[F(i == k) for k in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
+    result = []
+    for _ in range(end + 1):
+        result.append(power[0][0])
+        power = multiply(power, j)
+    return result
+
+
+def solve(a, b):
+    n = len(a)
+    z = [row[:] + [b[i]] for i, row in enumerate(a)]
+    for k in range(n):
+        pivot = next(i for i in range(k, n) if z[i][k])
+        z[k], z[pivot] = z[pivot], z[k]
+        scale = z[k][k]
+        z[k] = [u / scale for u in z[k]]
+        for i in range(n):
+            if i != k:
+                factor = z[i][k]
+                z[i] = [u - factor * v for u, v in zip(z[i], z[k])]
+    return [row[-1] for row in z]
+
+
+def check(m, gap):
+    a, b = matrix(m, gap), matrix(m, 2 * gap)
+    assert all(a[i][j] == b[i][j] for i in range(m) for j in range(m)
+               if (i, j) != (m - 1, m - 1))
+    # Positive local rows q_i = sigma_i^- - i/(i+1) sigma_(i+1)^-
+    # with weight (i+1)/i, plus gap*n_m, reproduce J exactly.
+    reconstructed = [[F(0) for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
+    for i in range(1, m):
+        weight = F(i + 1, i)
+        q = [F(0) for _ in range(m)]
+        q[i - 1], q[i] = F(1), -F(i, i + 1)
+        for x in range(m):
+            for y in range(m):
+                reconstructed[x][y] += weight * q[x] * q[y]
+    reconstructed[m - 1][m - 1] += gap
+    assert reconstructed == a
+
+    ma, mb = moments(a, 2 * m - 1), moments(b, 2 * m - 1)
+    assert ma[:2 * m - 1] == mb[:2 * m - 1]
+    assert mb[2 * m - 1] - ma[2 * m - 1] == gap
+    chi_a = solve(a, [F(1)] + [F(0)] * (m - 1))[0]
+    chi_b = solve(b, [F(1)] + [F(0)] * (m - 1))[0]
+    assert chi_a == F(m - 1, m) + 1 / (m * m * gap)
+    assert chi_b == F(m - 1, m) + 1 / (2 * m * m * gap)
+    return {
+        "m": m,
+        "gap_parameter": str(gap),
+        "identical_moments_through": 2 * m - 2,
+        "first_moment_difference": str(mb[-1] - ma[-1]),
+        "chi_low_terminal": str(chi_a),
+        "chi_high_terminal": str(chi_b),
+        "response_ratio": str(chi_a / chi_b),
+    }
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    print(json.dumps([check(m, F(1, 10**6)) for m in (3, 5, 8)], indent=2))

+# Follow-up: dual-template DNA-frame repair
+
+## Verdict
+
+A dual-template frame could support *sequence-agnostic, local repair* of a clean single-strand nick or short gap in either strand, provided the opposite strand is continuous across the gap, the damaged strand retains a usable upstream 3′-OH primer and downstream 5′-phosphate, and enzymes can reach the site. Polymerase copies the local sequence already present in the complementary strand; ligase closes the remaining nick. No site-specific repair oligo is needed.
+
+That is a plausible extension of existing DNA repair chemistry, not yet a demonstrated general repair operation for DNA origami. It does not repair an absent whole staple (there is no primer), a double-strand break, a gap in both strands, a damaged/missing template, or all common chemically blocked termini without additional end-processing enzymes. Standard origami also does not provide a continuous complementary strand along every routed segment. The idea becomes experimentally testable if designed as a 2D repair frame with continuous complementary corridors and crossovers kept outside the polymerase path. The largest independent physical gate is enzyme access in folded origami: ligase reaches a practical limit in 3D even for clean, designed nicks.
+
+## What has actually been shown
+
+Scheckenbach et al. demonstrated autonomous self-healing of damaged staples by adding an excess pool of matching staples; scaffold damage remained outside that mechanism. Their 0.2% serum assay also showed some nonspecific sacrificial-DNA protection, while 10% serum degradation was too fast for specific self-healing to dominate. This is a strong comparator, not evidence for template-directed repair of scaffold breaks ([2021 paper](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202012986), especially its discussion of scaffold limitation).
+
+Polymerase gap filling inside origami is already established for *designed* substrates. Agarwal et al. used T4 DNA polymerase to fill deliberately unpaired scaffold regions in wireframe structures; optimized filling took under 3 minutes and changed the structures’ shapes ([2018 paper](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.7b08345)). Yan et al. used Q5 polymerase to extend at designed allosteric sites at 37 °C for 5 hours and used T4 ligase to join designed split effector staples at 16 °C for 17 hours. The component operations therefore work in origami, but they were directed to designed sites and used separate reaction conditions; the paper does not establish a shared-bath repair of random strand damage ([2020 paper](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkaa488)).
+
+End chemistry, not just sequence complementarity, determines whether that extension-and-seal sequence can run:
+
+| Substrate at the damaged strand | Required operation |
+|---|---|
+| Clean nick, adjacent 3′-OH and 5′-phosphate | Ligase alone seals it; no nucleotide insertion is needed. |
+| Short single-strand gap, upstream 3′-OH and downstream 5′-phosphate | Polymerase extends the 3′ end using the opposite strand and dNTPs; ligase seals the final nick. |
+| 5′-OH end | Kinase activity plus ATP must first create a 5′-phosphate. |
+| 3′-phosphate or 3′-phosphoglycolate | A suitable 3′-phosphatase/end-cleanup activity is required to restore 3′-OH; some damage also deletes a nucleotide. |
+| Abasic site, oxidized base, crosslink, or blocked primer | Requires lesion-specific processing or can stall/miscode; generic gap fill alone is insufficient. |
+| Double-strand break, missing whole staple, or coincident gaps in both paired strands | No intact local template/primer pair; this operation cannot reconstruct it. |
+
+T4 DNA ligase specifically joins juxtaposed 3′-OH and 5′-phosphate ends. A primary in-vitro study showed mammalian PNK plus ligase I repairing 3′-phosphate/5′-OH nicks, and PNK + polymerase β + ligase I filling and sealing a 1-nt gap. The authors note that strand-break products have multiple terminal chemistries and must be restored to 3′-OH/5′-phosphate for synthesis and joining ([1998 NAR study](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/26.19.4395)). This supports end-processing as an achievable extension, but not an all-in-one origami cocktail.
+
+## Topology and crossovers
+
+In standard origami, one long scaffold is paired by many short staple segments. A staple can template repair of a local scaffold gap only where a staple segment spans the full gap and the polymerase’s path; the reverse is true for a gap in a staple. Staple ends and crossovers partition the complementary coverage. A double-stranded-scaffold origami has used both constituent strands in one integrated object, but its two paths are intentionally asymmetric and periodically converge; that architecture does not by itself prove uninterrupted, enzyme-accessible template coverage at every base ([2012 paper](https://doi.org/10.1021/nn302896c)).
+
+An origami crossover is a branched, four-strand junction. A polymerase can copy along its template strand in ordinary duplex DNA, but none of the repair demonstrations above establishes efficient polymerase transit through an origami crossover. Crossovers should therefore be outside the initial gap-repair corridor. If an arbitrary break lands at the junction, or the gap spans the crossover, repair and preservation of strand routing are unknown. Polymerase synthesizes a strand; it does not itself recreate a missing crossover or decide which alternate arm to follow.
+
+Covalent crosslinks can preserve a folded topology after nicks: Gerling et al. placed thymidines at strand termini and crossover sites, then UV-induced CPD bonds to point-weld strands. Crosslinked multilayer origami resisted heat, low-cation buffers, and nucleases, and retained its crossover network ([2018 Science Advances paper](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aau1157)). These links are structural constraints, not an information-bearing repair guide. A CPD is itself a DNA lesion and crosslinks near a repair tract may block polymerase or ligase; put them at frame anchors away from repair corridors and test enzyme access. Near-quantitative 2024 ligation work also identifies tight physical access as a limitation: T4 ligase plus 20% DMSO improved 2D nick sealing, while 3D origami required chemical CNBr ligation because the enzyme-access problem persisted ([2024 paper](https://doi.org/10.1002/smtd.202300999)).
+
+## Concrete achievable design
+
+Start with a **2D frame**, not a dense 3D object. Lay out one or more long, uninterrupted duplex repair corridors. Each corridor should have a continuous complementary template over at least the maximum test gap plus flanking bases, one accessible 3′-OH primer, and an adjacent 5′-phosphate on the damaged strand. Put crossovers and thymine crosslinks outside these corridors. Use a sequence with no intended lesion or secondary structure in the track. Include matched damaged substrates in which the gap is introduced separately into the scaffold-derived strand and the staple-derived strand.
+
+Run three substrates: (i) nick with 3′-OH/5′-phosphate; (ii) 1-, 3-, and 10-nt single-strand gaps with 3′-OH/5′-phosphate; (iii) blocked-end controls, 3′-phosphate and/or 5′-OH. Compare no enzyme, ligase only, polymerase only, polymerase + ligase, and end-cleanup + polymerase + ligase. Start with polymerase and ligase in sequential compatible buffers; separately test simultaneous incubation. A shared bath is a hypothesis because published origami work used a Q5 polymerase system at 37 °C and a T4 ligase system at 16 °C, while a later 2D ligation protocol used 37 °C, 0.5 mM ATP, 1× PNK buffer at pH 7.5, and 20% DMSO overnight. The DMSO ligation condition should not be assumed compatible with the polymerase. All staples in that ligation study were purified and 5′-phosphorylated before assembly; it was not repair of damaged sites in situ.
+
+For a sequence-agnostic test, prepare at least two equally frequent site variants or randomize the gap location across the corridor and do not provide repair oligos. Quantify strand-length restoration by denaturing PAGE or capillary electrophoresis, correct ligation by an end-specific assay, sequence the repaired tract, and measure frame retention by AFM or cryo-EM. Assay both the original and repaired substrate after a nuclease challenge. Report repair per eligible lesion and total frame yield; do not count only intact survivors. The critical negative controls are gaps without an opposite continuous template, damage at a crossover, and an otherwise identical 3D-packed structure.
+
+**Independent physical gate:** show that the enzyme actually reaches and traverses the designed corridor in the folded object. A practical success criterion is sequence-verified closure of ≥90% of accessible 1–3-nt clean gaps in each strand class, with no-template and crossover-spanning controls near background, while retaining the frame geometry. Then vary corridor depth/packing to map access loss. Failure in 3D would limit the claim to 2D or exposed corridors, regardless of a successful solution-phase duplex assay.
+
+## Claim boundary
+
+If the gate passes, the result would be random-location repair of *eligible single-strand gaps* in a deliberately redundant DNA frame, using generic enzymes and dNTPs rather than a sequence-specific oligo pool. It would not show general repair of arbitrary random molecular damage, every staple or scaffold loss, or autonomous repair without energetic/material inputs. Polymerization consumes dNTPs; ligation consumes ATP, and end cleanup may consume ATP. Any energy/throughput advantage over matching-staple replacement must count those reagents, enzymes, preprocessing, folding, purification, and measured repair yield against a matched incumbent. No such full-cost advantage is established here.
+
+## Primary references
+
+- Scheckenbach et al., “Self-Regeneration and Self-Healing in DNA Origami Nanostructures,” *Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.* 2021, DOI: [10.1002/anie.202012986](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202012986).
+- Agarwal et al., “Structural Transformation of Wireframe DNA Origami via DNA Polymerase Assisted Gap-Filling,” *ACS Nano* 2018, DOI: [10.1021/acsnano.7b08345](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.7b08345).
+- Yan et al., “Allostery of DNA nanostructures controlled by enzymatic modifications,” *Nucleic Acids Research* 2020, DOI: [10.1093/nar/gkaa488](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkaa488).
+- Yang et al., “DNA Origami with Double-Stranded DNA as a Unified Scaffold,” *ACS Nano* 2012, DOI: [10.1021/nn302896c](https://doi.org/10.1021/nn302896c).
+- Gerling et al., “Sequence-programmable covalent bonding of designed DNA assemblies,” *Science Advances* 2018, DOI: [10.1126/sciadv.aau1157](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aau1157).
+- Krishnamurthy et al., “Near Quantitative Ligation Results in Resistance of DNA Origami Against Nuclease and Cell Lysate,” *Small Methods* 2024, DOI: [10.1002/smtd.202300999](https://doi.org/10.1002/smtd.202300999).
